\chapter{La herramienta}
\label{ch:es-pedir}
\hlchaptermodality{460}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can borrow a tool from a shared store: read the notice, apply the way the form wants, and understand that there is a waiting list.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la herramienta]{la herramienta — the tool}

\label{lesson:ES-C460-herramienta}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el taladro} and \textbf{arreglar}. The drill is one of these; name the category it belongs to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la herramienta}
\textbf{la herramienta} — the tool.

\emph{Una caja de herramientas} — a toolbox. \emph{No tengo las herramientas} — I haven't got the tools. \emph{La herramienta adecuada} — the right tool for the job.

It covers the abstract sense as well: \emph{una herramienta muy útil} about an app or a method, exactly as English uses \textquotedblleft{}tool\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the h that hides a diphthong}]
Say it: \textbf{e-rra-MIEN-ta}. The \textbf{h} is silent, as it is anywhere in Spanish that it stands alone, and underneath it is the \textbf{ie} you have met before:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
ferramenta & la h\textbf{e}rramienta \\
ferrum & el h\textbf{ie}rro \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One rule governs both vowels, and it is the one you already have: a stressed \textbf{e} breaks, an unstressed one stays flat. In \emph{ferrum} the stress is on the \textbf{e}, so it breaks — \emph{h\textbf{ie}rro}. In \emph{ferramenta} the stress has moved onto the suffix, so the first \textbf{e} stays flat — \emph{h\textbf{e}rra-} — and the break happens where the stress went instead: \emph{-m\textbf{ie}nta}, the very same \emph{-miento} you have in \emph{el seguimiento}.

The \textbf{h} is written because it was once spoken. Latin \emph{f-} weakened to a breathy \emph{h} in Castilian mouths, the breath faded, and the spelling stayed behind. That \emph{f}-to-\emph{h} shift is one of the loudest things Spanish did to Latin.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{ferramenta}, \textquotedblleft{}things made of iron\textquotedblright{} — the plural of \emph{ferramentum}, from \textbf{ferrum}, iron.

So a \emph{herramienta} is an \textbf{iron thing}, and the name is older than any of the tools you own. The same \emph{ferrum} is the \textbf{Fe} on the periodic table, and it gives Spanish \emph{el hierro}, \emph{el herrero} — the blacksmith — and \emph{la herradura}, a horseshoe.

That \textbf{f} to \textbf{h} is the signature of Spanish among the Romance languages. Latin \emph{facere} gave \emph{hacer}, \emph{filius} gave \emph{hijo}, \emph{ferrum} gave \emph{hierro} — while Italian kept \emph{ferro} and French kept \emph{fer}. The letter is silent now, but it marks where an \emph{f} used to be.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a toolbox, and the right tool
  \item the drill is a tool
  \item which letter \emph{hierro} and \emph{hacer} both used to start with
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The tool? (\textbf{La herramienta}.) What is \emph{ferrum}? (\textbf{Iron}.) What does a silent Spanish \textbf{h} often mark? (\textbf{Where a Latin f used to be}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[solicitar]{solicitar — the word the form uses}

\label{lesson:ES-C460-solicitar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la cita} and \textbf{entregar}. Both belong to the same morning at a counter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: solicitar}
\textbf{solicitar} — to apply for, to request, formally.

\begin{quote}
Para \textbf{solicitar} una plaza, entregue la ficha antes del día 20.
\end{quote}

\emph{Solicitar una beca} — to apply for a grant. \emph{Solicitar cita previa} — to book an appointment in advance, the phrase on Spanish health-centre and town-hall pages; much of Latin America says \emph{sacar turno} or \emph{agendar una cita} for the same act.

\textbf{La solicitud} is the application itself, and the piece of paper it is written on.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: solicitar is not pedir}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you are doing} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
asking a person for a thing & \textbf{pedir} \\
asking an institution, on a form & \textbf{solicitar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Le pido un café al camarero.} \emph{Solicito una beca al ministerio.} Using \emph{solicitar} with a friend would sound as though you had filled in a form to borrow their drill.

That is the whole difference and it is register, not meaning: \emph{solicitar} is the bookish arrival, worn nowhere down, and it belongs to writing.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{sollicitare}: \textbf{sollus}, whole, plus \textbf{citare}, to set in motion — so to stir something \emph{entirely}, to shake it up.

The oldest sense is agitation, and Spanish keeps that branch too: \emph{estar solícito} is to be attentive, and English \textbf{solicitous} means anxiously caring, while \textbf{solicitude} is worry. To apply for something is to set the machinery in motion on your behalf.

That \textbf{citare} is the one inside \textbf{la cita} — an appointment is a \emph{summoning} — and English \textbf{cite}, \textbf{excite}, \textbf{recite} and \textbf{incite} are all the same setting-in-motion.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to apply for a place, hand the form in
  \item book an appointment in advance
  \item which verb you use with a waiter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To apply for? (\textbf{Solicitar}.) The application? (\textbf{La solicitud}.) What does \emph{citare} mean? (\textbf{To set in motion, to summon}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la espera]{la espera — the wait}

\label{lesson:ES-C460-espera}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{esperar} and \textbf{el plazo}. One is the doing, one is the window. The noun between them is next.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la espera}
\textbf{la espera} — the wait.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Sala de espera.}
\end{quote}

\emph{La lista de espera} — the waiting list. \emph{Una espera de dos horas} — a two-hour wait. \emph{En espera de su respuesta} — awaiting your reply, the closing line of a formal letter.

The verb you already have; this is the noun that goes on the door.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a noun made by cutting, not by adding}]
You have four noun-making suffixes — three that work on verbs, and \emph{-eza}, which works on adjectives. This is a fifth move, and it is the opposite of all of them: \textbf{take the ending off}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{noun} \\
\midrule
esperar & la esper\textbf{a} \\
entregar & la entreg\textbf{a} \\
comprar & la compr\textbf{a} \\
pagar & el pag\textbf{o} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Cut \emph{-ar} and put back a bare \textbf{-a} or \textbf{-o}. You already have one of these: \emph{la entrega} arrived two chapters ago without being named as a pattern. These are the shortest nouns in the language and among the commonest. What you cannot predict is \textbf{which vowel} a given verb will take — \emph{la compra} but \emph{el pago}. Once you have the word, the ordinary \emph{-o}/\emph{-a} rule hands you the article as usual.

Set beside \emph{la solicitud}: one verb swaps its ending for \emph{-ud}, the other drops its ending and puts back a single vowel. Both are ordinary.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{sperare}, from \textbf{spes}, hope — though already in Latin it leaned as much on \emph{looking forward to} as on hoping, and a Roman could \emph{sperare} bad news as readily as good.

That middle sense is the hinge. \emph{Esperar} took over the work of Latin \emph{exspectare}, \textbf{to expect}, and ended up covering all three English verbs you met when you learned it: \emph{espero el autobús} is waiting, \emph{espero el pan} is expecting, \emph{espero que sí} is hoping. \emph{La espera} names only the first of them.

You met the same root in \textbf{la esperanza}, hope, which is \emph{-anza} on this verb. So \emph{la espera} and \emph{la esperanza} are one word twice: the plain wait, and the hope that grew out of it.

The \textbf{e-} at the front is Spanish's own, the same one that turned \emph{stare} into \emph{estar} and \emph{stroppiare} into \emph{estropear}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the waiting room and the waiting list
  \item I'm waiting for the bus, then I hope so
  \item what \emph{la espera} and \emph{la esperanza} share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The wait? (\textbf{La espera}.) The waiting room? (\textbf{La sala de espera}.) What else does \emph{esperar} cover? (\textbf{Hoping and expecting}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(la herramienta, solicitar, la espera)]{(la herramienta, solicitar, la espera) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R460-repaso-pedir}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all three: \emph{the tool}, \emph{to apply for}, \emph{the wait}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: five ways to a noun, now complete}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{how} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{gender} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-anza} & la mudanza & feminine \\
\textbf{-miento} & el seguimiento & masculine \\
\textbf{-eza} & la limpieza & feminine \\
\textbf{-ción} & la instalación & feminine \\
\textbf{cut the ending} & la espera & either \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The first four hand you the article. \textbf{The fifth does not} — \emph{la espera}, \emph{la compra}, but \emph{el pago} and \emph{el gasto} — so a cut-ending noun is the one kind where the gender has to be learned with the word.

Note what that costs: these are the shortest and commonest nouns in Spanish, and they are the ones the endings cannot help you with.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two of the three were relatives}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{new word} & \textbf{what it was built on} \\
\midrule
\textbf{la herramienta} & \emph{ferrum}, iron — and \emph{el hierro} \\
\textbf{solicitar} & \emph{citare}, inside \emph{la cita} \\
\textbf{la espera} & \emph{esperar}, and \emph{la esperanza} beside it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{La espera} is the neat one: \textbf{esperar} and \textbf{la esperanza} arrived together with the verb itself, long ago, and the moving chapter showed you the \emph{-anza} that builds the second from the first. This is the third member — the plain noun that sits between the verb and the abstract one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the waiting room is that way
  \item to apply for a place you hand in the form
  \item which of the five noun-makers leaves the gender open
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All three again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence asking for something at a counter.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(pedir prestada una herramienta) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C460-sintesis-pedir}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la herramienta} and \textbf{solicitar}. The notice below uses one for the things and one for the paperwork.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A notice in a neighbourhood centre. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{PRÉSTAMO DE HERRAMIENTAS}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Taladros, escaleras y carritos. Dos días por vecino.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Para \textbf{solicitar} una \textbf{herramienta}, rellene la ficha en conserjería.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Hay \textbf{lista de espera} para el taladro grande.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what you can borrow, and for how long
  \item what you have to do to ask for one
  \item which item you may not get straight away
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Solicitar} on a noticeboard and \textbf{pedir} at the counter are the same act in two registers. The notice says \emph{para solicitar una herramienta} because it is describing a procedure; the neighbour who walks in says \emph{¿me dejas el taladro?} That pair is the whole of Spanish formality in one scene.

\textbf{Hay lista de espera} — bare, with no article at all. The firm rule is what \emph{hay} refuses: never \emph{hay la lista}, because \emph{hay} introduces a thing's existence rather than pointing at one already known. Between \emph{hay lista} and \emph{hay una lista} both are correct, and the bare noun is what a notice board uses.

And \textbf{por vecino} — \textquotedblleft{}per neighbour\textquotedblright{} — is \emph{por} doing distribution, the same \emph{por} that gave a cause on the roadworks sign. One preposition, several jobs, and the noun after it stays bare.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines for a tool library: say what is lent and for how long, say how to apply, say there is a waiting list, and then ask a neighbour informally for the same thing.

Then check yourself: did the notice use \emph{solicitar} and the neighbour \emph{pedir}?
\end{tcolorbox}
